opus-5.5.text:
I usually start by asking where the real bottleneck is, not which problem looks most interesting on paper. LLM infrastructure has an endless list of possible research directions, like scheduling, memory management, kernels, quantization, distributed serving, and programming abstractions. If you chase all of them you spread yourself too thin. So I try to look at actual workloads and see what's really limiting people. Sometimes it's GPU memory, sometimes it's redundant computation across requests, and sometimes it's just that developers have no good way to express what they want the system to do.

A lot of my work came from noticing patterns in how people actually use these models. For example, more and more applications aren't a single prompt and a single response. They're programs: multiple calls, branching, shared prefixes, structured outputs. Once you see that, you realize the system should exploit that structure. That's the thinking behind ideas like reusing the KV cache across requests with a radix tree, or co-designing the frontend language with the runtime. The research problem fell out of watching the workload.

Second, I care a lot about building real systems that people use. In infrastructure it's easy to write a paper with a nice speedup on a benchmark you designed yourself. The harder test is whether it holds up when thousands of users run it in production with messy, diverse workloads. Open-source has been really valuable for that. The community tells you very quickly what matters and what doesn't, and that feedback loop shapes which problems I prioritize next.

Third, I try to balance short-term and long-term work. Some problems are urgent: a new model architecture comes out and you need to support it efficiently right away. Others are more fundamental, like how to think about scheduling or memory hierarchy as models and hardware keep changing. I want to keep doing both, because the urgent engineering keeps you grounded and the fundamental questions keep you from just chasing the latest release.

And finally, collaboration. These problems cut across machine learning, systems, compilers, and hardware, and no single person has all that expertise. A lot of the best ideas I've been part of came from people with different backgrounds sitting together and realizing a problem looks very different from the other side.

r001.rationale: The response says there are many possible directions and that chasing all of them spreads effort thin, but it does not clearly say to work through the problems one at a time.

r002.rationale: The response discusses its own way of choosing problems, but does not say that many researchers recognize the same problems or that these are not uniquely apparent to Ying Sheng.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the way I approach it is pretty bottom-up. I don't usually start from a grand theory of what LLM infrastructure should look like. I start from pain. When we were building systems like FlexGen and later SGLang, almost every research problem came from someone actually trying to run a model and hitting a wall: the GPU memory runs out, the throughput is terrible, the prompt cache is being thrown away between requests, the scheduler is doing something dumb. Those walls are the research agenda.

So the first filter I apply is: is this a real bottleneck that real users feel today, or is it a bottleneck I can imagine on a whiteboard? There are many problems in this space, and a lot of them are interesting in the abstract but either disappear with the next hardware generation or only matter at a scale no one actually operates at. I try to pick the ones where, if I solve it, someone's job gets easier next month, not in three years.

The second thing is that I think of the stack as a whole rather than as isolated layers. In LLM serving, the model architecture, the attention kernel, the memory manager, the scheduler, and even the frontend programming interface are all coupled. A lot of the wins in SGLang came not from one clever kernel but from co-designing the frontend language with the runtime, so that the runtime can see structure like shared prefixes or branching that a plain text API would hide. If you only look at one layer, you miss those opportunities.

And the third part is that I rely heavily on the open-source community to tell me what matters. When you put a system out there and thousands of people run it, the issues they file are basically a ranked list of research problems. Some of them are boring engineering, but a surprising number are genuinely open questions. So I don't feel I have to choose problems alone. The users choose a lot of them for me, and my job is to recognize which ones have a deep idea hiding behind what looks like a bug report.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes identifying many problems and prioritizing real bottlenecks, but does not say they are quickly recognized and then worked through one at a time.

r002.rationale: The candidate says users and the open-source community surface problems, but does not state that many researchers recognize the same problems or that Ying Sheng's recognition is not unique.

astra-6.text:
I try to start with the bottleneck. There are so many interesting problems in LLM infrastructure, but the first question is: which one actually matters for the workload we’re trying to support? Is it memory, compute, communication, or how requests are scheduled?

Then I try to turn that into a concrete research question. Can we isolate the problem, understand why existing approaches fall short, and test an idea against a meaningful baseline? I like to start with a small experiment that tells us whether the intuition is right before building a complicated system.

And I think you have to keep revisiting your assumptions. Models change, hardware changes, and the way people use models changes. So the goal is to solve an important problem today while understanding the underlying principle well enough that the work remains useful as the system evolves.

r001.rationale: The response says to identify a bottleneck and develop a concrete research question, but it does not communicate the contrast between quickly recognizing many problems and working through them one at a time.

r002.rationale: It mentions many interesting infrastructure problems, but does not say those problems are apparent to many researchers or that Ying Sheng is not unique in recognizing them.

sol-6.1.text:
I try to start with the bottleneck: what is actually preventing the system from being faster, cheaper, or easier to use? There are so many interesting research problems that you need a way to prioritize them. For me, that means connecting a technical question to a concrete workload and asking how much solving it would matter.

Then I like to build something small and measure it. Sometimes the experiment tells you that your original assumption was wrong, or that improving one component just moves the bottleneck somewhere else. That’s why I think it’s important to look at the whole system and keep iterating between the research idea and what happens in practice.

r001.rationale: The response says there are many interesting problems and describes prioritizing and testing them, but does not contrast quickly recognizing many problems with working through them one at a time.

r002.rationale: It does not say that these problems are apparent to many researchers or that Ying Sheng’s recognition is not unique.
